Wave equation

What you will learn

  • The wave equation uxx=utt/v2u_{xx} = u_{tt}/v^2uxx​=utt​/v2 is a linear second-order PDE. Any sum of solutions is again a solution, so the general solution can be assembled from simple building blocks.

  • Boundary conditions (what the wave does at the edges) and initial conditions (its shape and velocity at t=0t=0t=0) turn the general solution into the one solution that describes a particular system.

  • Separation of variables, u(x,t)=X(x)T(t)u(x,t)=X(x)T(t)u(x,t)=X(x)T(t), splits the PDE into two ordinary differential equations that we solve with an exponential trial function.

  • Fixed ends quantize. For a string of length LLL the boundary conditions allow only the normal modes sin⁡(nπx/L)\sin(n\pi x/L)sin(nπx/L) with integer nnn, each oscillating at its own frequency ωn=nπv/L\omega_n = n\pi v/Lωn​=nπv/L.

  • Any motion of the string is a sum of normal modes, with amplitudes set by the initial pluck. In two dimensions the same recipe gives modes labeled by two integers and introduces degeneracy.

Classical wave equation¶

  • The wave equation is a second-order PDE (partial differential equation) that governs the displacement u(x,t)u(x,t)u(x,t) in time and space:

∂2u(x,t)∂x2=1v2∂2u(x,t)∂t2\frac{\partial^2 u(x,t)}{\partial x^2 }= \frac{1}{v^2}\frac{\partial^2 u(x,t)}{\partial t^2}∂x2∂2u(x,t)​=v21​∂t2∂2u(x,t)​
(1)

  • In the previous lecture we saw that any right-moving shape f(x−vt)f(x-vt)f(x−vt) and any left-moving shape g(x+vt)g(x+vt)g(x+vt) solve it, and so does the sum f(x−vt)+g(x+vt)f(x-vt)+g(x+vt)f(x−vt)+g(x+vt). This is enough to predict the future of a wave on an infinite string once we know its starting shape and starting velocity. A bump released from rest, for example, must split into two half-height copies running in opposite directions, because that is the only combination of fff and ggg that starts with zero velocity everywhere.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
f = lambda s: np.exp(-s**2 / 0.5)
v = 1.0
x = np.linspace(-8, 8, 1000)
ts = np.linspace(0, 5.5, 40)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.8))
ax.plot(x, f(x), color=GRAY, lw=1.2, ls=":", label="initial shape f(x), released from rest")
(hr,) = ax.plot([], [], color=TEAL, lw=1.6, ls="--", label=r"$\frac{1}{2}f(x-vt)$")
(hl,) = ax.plot([], [], color=ORANGE, lw=1.6, ls="--", label=r"$\frac{1}{2}f(x+vt)$")
(u,) = ax.plot([], [], color=CARDINAL, lw=2.8, label="u(x, t)")
ax.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.6)
ax.set_xlim(-8, 8); ax.set_ylim(-0.1, 1.3); ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("u")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False, fontsize=9.5)
ax.set_title(r"the wave equation splits a bump in two:  $u = \frac{1}{2}[f(x-vt) + f(x+vt)]$",
             loc="left", fontsize=11.5)
fig.tight_layout()

def update(i):
    t = ts[i]
    hr.set_data(x, 0.5 * f(x - v * t)); hl.set_data(x, 0.5 * f(x + v * t))
    u.set_data(x, 0.5 * (f(x - v * t) + f(x + v * t)))

ani = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=len(ts), interval=100, blit=False)
plt.close(fig)
HTML(ani.to_jshtml())

Fig. A Gaussian bump released from rest on an infinite string. The wave equation carries half of it to the right and half to the left; the sum (red) is the string’s actual shape at each instant.

  • Real strings are not infinite. A guitar string is clamped at both ends, and the clamps change everything: traveling waves reflect back and forth, and only certain shapes survive. Solving the wave equation on a finite string is the task of this lecture. The pattern of the solution, boundary conditions produce integers, is exactly what we will meet again in the Schrödinger equation.

Solving the wave equation: the big picture¶

  • 1. Boundary conditions. For a string of length LLL fixed at both ends, the displacement must vanish at the clamps at all times:

u(0,t)=0andu(L,t)=0u(0, t) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad u(L, t) = 0u(0,t)=0andu(L,t)=0
(2)

  • 2. Separation of variables. We look for solutions in which the dependence on xxx and on ttt factorizes, u(x,t)=X(x) T(t)u(x, t) = X(x) \, T(t)u(x,t)=X(x)T(t). Such a product is a standing wave: a fixed shape X(x)X(x)X(x) whose overall height T(t)T(t)T(t) oscillates. This guess turns the PDE into two ordinary differential equations (ODEs), one for each variable.

  • 3. Principle of superposition. The wave equation is linear (uuu appears to the first power on both sides), so any linear combination of solutions is a solution. Once we have found all the separable solutions un=Xn(x)Tn(t)u_n = X_n(x)T_n(t)un​=Xn​(x)Tn​(t), the general solution is their sum:

u=∑ncnunu = \sum_n c_n u_nu=n∑​cn​un​
(3)

Step 1: Plug the product X(x)T(t)X(x)T(t)X(x)T(t) into the wave equation¶

  • Substitute u(x,t)=X(x)T(t)u(x, t) = X(x)T(t)u(x,t)=X(x)T(t) into the wave equation:

1v2∂2u∂t2=∂2u∂x2\frac{1}{v^2}\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}v21​∂t2∂2u​=∂x2∂2u​
(4)

  • Since XXX does not depend on ttt and TTT does not depend on xxx, each partial derivative acts on one factor only:

X(x)v2d2Tdt2=T(t)d2Xdx2\frac{X(x)}{v^2}\frac{d^2 T}{d t^2} = T(t)\frac{d^2 X}{d x^2}v2X(x)​dt2d2T​=T(t)dx2d2X​
(5)

  • Divide both sides by X(x)T(t)X(x)T(t)X(x)T(t):

1v2 T(t)d2Tdt2=1X(x)d2Xdx2\frac{1}{v^2\, T(t)}\frac{d^2 T}{d t^2} = \frac{1}{X(x)}\frac{d^2 X}{d x^2}v2T(t)1​dt2d2T​=X(x)1​dx2d2X​
(6)

  • The left side depends only on ttt and the right side only on xxx. A function of ttt alone can equal a function of xxx alone for all xxx and ttt only if both are the same constant, which we call KKK:

1v2 Td2Tdt2=1Xd2Xdx2=K\frac{1}{v^2\, T}\frac{d^2 T}{d t^2} = \frac{1}{X}\frac{d^2 X}{d x^2} = Kv2T1​dt2d2T​=X1​dx2d2X​=K
(7)

  • One PDE has become two ODEs:

d2Xdx2−KX=0,d2Tdt2−Kv2 T=0\frac{d^2 X}{d x^2} - K X = 0, \qquad \frac{d^2 T}{d t^2} - K v^2\, T = 0dx2d2X​−KX=0,dt2d2T​−Kv2T=0
(8)

Step 2: Solve each ordinary differential equation¶

Solving linear, homogeneous ODEs with constant coefficients

From an ODE to an algebraic equation

  • An ODE is linear if yyy and its derivatives appear only to the first power, and homogeneous if the right-hand side is zero. For such equations the trial function y(x)=erxy(x) = e^{rx}y(x)=erx works, because every derivative of erxe^{rx}erx is a multiple of erxe^{rx}erx.

  • Plugging it in and cancelling the common factor erxe^{rx}erx leaves an algebraic equation for rrr, the characteristic equation. For a second-order ODE it is a quadratic:

ay′′+by′+cy=0⟶ar2+br+c=0,r1,2=−b±b2−4ac2aa y^{''} + by^{'} + cy = 0 \quad \longrightarrow \quad ar^2 + br + c = 0, \qquad r_{1,2} = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}ay′′+by′+cy=0⟶ar2+br+c=0,r1,2​=2a−b±b2−4ac​​
(9)

  • The general solution is a linear combination of the two exponentials. Two extra pieces of information (boundary or initial conditions) fix c1c_1c1​ and c2c_2c2​:

y(x)=c1er1x+c2er2xy(x) = c_1e^{r_1 x}+c_2 e^{r_2 x}y(x)=c1​er1​x+c2​er2​x
(10)

Example

d2ydx2+4y=0⟶r2+4=0⟶r=±2i\frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} +4y = 0 \quad \longrightarrow \quad r^2 + 4 = 0 \quad \longrightarrow \quad r=\pm 2idx2d2y​+4y=0⟶r2+4=0⟶r=±2i
(11)
y=c1e2ix+c2e−2ix=C1cos⁡(2x)+C2sin⁡(2x)y=c_1e^{2ix} + c_2e^{-2ix} = C_1\cos(2x) + C_2\sin(2x)y=c1​e2ix+c2​e−2ix=C1​cos(2x)+C2​sin(2x)
(12)

  • Complex roots r=±iβr = \pm i\betar=±iβ always mean oscillation, and Euler’s formula converts the complex exponentials into sines and cosines with new real constants C1C_1C1​, C2C_2C2​. Real roots mean exponential growth or decay; a repeated root gives (c1+c2x)erx(c_1 + c_2 x)e^{rx}(c1​+c2​x)erx.

The damped oscillator, y′′+2βy′+ω2y=0y'' + 2\beta y' + \omega^2 y = 0y′′+2βy′+ω2y=0, shows what the root type means for the motion. Its characteristic equation has roots r=−β±β2−ω2r = -\beta \pm \sqrt{\beta^2 - \omega^2}r=−β±β2−ω2​: complex when the damping is weak, real when it is strong. The full solution is worked out in Problem 2 at the end of the chapter.

# synced: damped_oscillator
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
w, b_under, b_over = 2 * np.pi, 0.45, 5.0 * np.pi          # omega, weak and strong damping
t = np.linspace(0, 4, 400)
ts = np.linspace(0, 4, 40)
wd = np.sqrt(w**2 - b_under**2)
y_under = np.exp(-b_under * t) * (np.cos(wd * t) + (b_under / wd) * np.sin(wd * t))
r1, r2 = -b_over + np.sqrt(b_over**2 - w**2), -b_over - np.sqrt(b_over**2 - w**2)
y_over = (r2 * np.exp(r1 * t) - r1 * np.exp(r2 * t)) / (r2 - r1)
y_crit = (1 + w * t) * np.exp(-w * t)
YLO, YHI, TOP = -1.3, 1.95, 1.85                             # shared y range, spring anchor

spring_xy = lambda y_mass, n=9, half=0.16: (                # zigzag from the anchor to the mass
    np.concatenate([[0.0], half * (-1.0) ** np.arange(2 * n), [0.0]]),
    np.linspace(TOP, y_mass + 0.14, 2 * n + 2))

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8, 3.2))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(1, 4, width_ratios=[1, 3.4, 1, 3.4], wspace=0.32)
ax_s1, ax1, ax_s2, ax2 = [fig.add_subplot(gs[0, i]) for i in range(4)]
for ax_s, fluid, col in ((ax_s1, "water", "#d6ecf5"), (ax_s2, "honey", "#f4d9a4")):
    ax_s.set_xlim(-0.6, 0.6); ax_s.set_ylim(YLO, YHI); ax_s.set_axis_off()
    ax_s.fill_between([-0.6, 0.6], YLO, TOP + 0.02, color=col, zorder=0)
    ax_s.plot([-0.5, 0.5], [TOP, TOP], color="k", lw=3)
    ax_s.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.8, ls=":")
    ax_s.text(0, YLO + 0.12, fluid, ha="center", fontsize=10.5, color="#444444")
for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.8)
    ax.set_xlim(0, 4); ax.set_ylim(YLO, YHI); ax.set_xlabel("t / T"); ax.set_yticks([-1, 0, 1])
ax1.plot(t, np.exp(-b_under * t), color=GRAY, lw=1, ls="--")
ax1.plot(t, -np.exp(-b_under * t), color=GRAY, lw=1, ls="--")
ax1.text(2.4, 0.5, r"$\pm e^{-\beta t}$", color=GRAY, fontsize=10)
ax1.set_title(r"complex roots $r=-\beta\pm i\omega_d$: oscillates, decays", loc="left", fontsize=10)
ax2.plot(t, y_crit, color=GRAY, lw=1.2, ls="--")
ax2.text(1.1, 0.42, "critical", color=GRAY, fontsize=10)
ax2.set_title(r"real roots $r_1, r_2<0$: no oscillation", loc="left", fontsize=10)
(l1,) = ax1.plot([], [], color=TEAL, lw=2.4)
(d1,) = ax1.plot([], [], "o", color=TEAL, ms=8, mec="white", mew=1.2, zorder=5)
(l2,) = ax2.plot([], [], color=CARDINAL, lw=2.4)
(d2,) = ax2.plot([], [], "o", color=CARDINAL, ms=8, mec="white", mew=1.2, zorder=5)
(sp1,) = ax_s1.plot([], [], color="#444444", lw=1.4)
(m1,) = ax_s1.plot([], [], "s", color=TEAL, ms=15, mec="white", mew=1.2, zorder=5)
(sp2,) = ax_s2.plot([], [], color="#444444", lw=1.4)
(m2,) = ax_s2.plot([], [], "s", color=CARDINAL, ms=15, mec="white", mew=1.2, zorder=5)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.02, right=0.985, top=0.88, bottom=0.18)

def update(i):
    n = int(np.searchsorted(t, ts[i])) + 1
    yu, yo = y_under[n - 1], y_over[n - 1]
    l1.set_data(t[:n], y_under[:n]); d1.set_data([t[n - 1]], [yu])
    l2.set_data(t[:n], y_over[:n]); d2.set_data([t[n - 1]], [yo])
    sp1.set_data(*spring_xy(yu)); m1.set_data([0], [yu])
    sp2.set_data(*spring_xy(yo)); m2.set_data([0], [yo])

ani = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=len(ts), interval=100, blit=False)
plt.close(fig)
HTML(ani.to_jshtml())

Fig. A mass on a spring released in water (left) and in honey (right). Left: complex roots r=−β±iωdr = -\beta \pm i\omega_dr=−β±iωd​ give an oscillation inside a decaying envelope; the imaginary part sets the frequency, the real part the decay. Right: two real negative roots give decay with no oscillation, the dashed curve being the critically damped case. The spatial equation X′′−KX=0X'' - KX = 0X′′−KX=0 faces the same fork, decided by the sign of KKK.

Solving the spatial part when K>0K > 0K>0

  • If K>0K > 0K>0, write K=β2K = \beta^2K=β2. The characteristic equation r2−β2=0r^2 - \beta^2 = 0r2−β2=0 has real roots r=±βr = \pm\betar=±β, so

    X(x)=c1eβx+c2e−βxX(x) = c_1 e^{\beta x} + c_2 e^{-\beta x}X(x)=c1​eβx+c2​e−βx
    (13)

  • Apply the boundary conditions. X(0)=0X(0) = 0X(0)=0 gives c2=−c1c_2 = -c_1c2​=−c1​, and then X(L)=c1(eβL−e−βL)=0X(L) = c_1\left(e^{\beta L} - e^{-\beta L}\right) = 0X(L)=c1​(eβL−e−βL)=0 forces c1=0c_1 = 0c1​=0, because the bracket is not zero for βL≠0\beta L \neq 0βL=0. Only the trivial solution survives:

    X(x)=0X(x) = 0X(x)=0
    (14)

  • A string that does not move makes no music. Growing and decaying exponentials cannot be pinned to zero at both ends; positive KKK is ruled out.

Solving the spatial part when K<0K < 0K<0

  • If K<0K < 0K<0, write K=−β2K = -\beta^2K=−β2. The characteristic equation r2+β2=0r^2 + \beta^2 = 0r2+β2=0 has imaginary roots r=±iβr = \pm i\betar=±iβ:

    X(x)=c1eiβx+c2e−iβxX(x) = c_1 e^{i \beta x} + c_2 e^{-i \beta x}X(x)=c1​eiβx+c2​e−iβx
    (15)

  • Using Euler’s formula, e±iβx=cos⁡(βx)±isin⁡(βx)e^{\pm i\beta x} = \cos(\beta x) \pm i \sin(\beta x)e±iβx=cos(βx)±isin(βx), and collecting terms:

    X(x)=(c1+c2)cos⁡(βx)+i(c1−c2)sin⁡(βx)=Acos⁡(βx)+Bsin⁡(βx)X(x) = (c_1 + c_2) \cos(\beta x) + i(c_1 - c_2) \sin(\beta x) = A \cos(\beta x) + B \sin(\beta x)X(x)=(c1​+c2​)cos(βx)+i(c1​−c2​)sin(βx)=Acos(βx)+Bsin(βx)
    (16)

  • Apply the boundary conditions:

    • At x=0x = 0x=0: X(0)=A⋅1+B⋅0=0X(0) = A \cdot 1 + B \cdot 0 = 0X(0)=A⋅1+B⋅0=0, so A=0A = 0A=0.

    • At x=Lx = Lx=L: X(L)=Bsin⁡(βL)=0X(L) = B \sin(\beta L) = 0X(L)=Bsin(βL)=0.

  • For a non-trivial solution B≠0B \neq 0B=0, so we need sin⁡(βL)=0\sin(\beta L) = 0sin(βL)=0. The sine vanishes only at integer multiples of π\piπ:

    βL=nπ⟹βn=nπL,n=1,2,3,…\beta L = n \pi \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \beta_n = \frac{n \pi}{L}, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldotsβL=nπ⟹βn​=Lnπ​,n=1,2,3,…
    (17)

  • The boundary conditions have quantized β\betaβ. Every allowed value gives one solution:

    Xn(x)=Bnsin⁡(nπxL)X_n(x) = B_n \sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{L} \right)Xn​(x)=Bn​sin(Lnπx​)
    (18)

  • The value n=0n = 0n=0 gives X=0X = 0X=0 and negative nnn only flips the sign of BnB_nBn​, so the distinct solutions are n=1,2,3,…n = 1, 2, 3, \ldotsn=1,2,3,…

x = np.linspace(0, L, 400)

for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.8)

ax1.legend(loc="upper center", fontsize=10, frameon=False, ncol=2)
for n, c in ((1, TEAL), (2, PURPLE)):

Fig. Why the sign of KKK decides. Left: for K>0K > 0K>0 the solutions are growing and decaying exponentials, and no combination of them returns to zero at both clamps. Right: for K<0K < 0K<0 the solutions are sines and cosines, and the sines vanish at both clamps whenever a whole number of half-wavelengths fits.

Solving the temporal part

  • The spatial part has forced K=−βn2K = -\beta_n^2K=−βn2​ with βn=nπ/L\beta_n = n\pi/Lβn​=nπ/L. Insert this into the time ODE:

d2Tdt2−Kv2 T=0⟹d2Tdt2+βn2v2 T=0\frac{d^2 T}{d t^2} - K v^2\, T = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \frac{d^2 T}{d t^2} + \beta_n^2 v^2\, T = 0dt2d2T​−Kv2T=0⟹dt2d2T​+βn2​v2T=0
(19)

  • This is the harmonic-oscillator equation with characteristic roots r=±iβnvr = \pm i\beta_n vr=±iβn​v. Its solution oscillates at the angular frequency ωn=βnv\omega_n = \beta_n vωn​=βn​v:

Tn(t)=Dncos⁡(ωnt)+Ensin⁡(ωnt),ωn=βnv=nπvLT_n(t) = D_n \cos(\omega_n t) + E_n \sin(\omega_n t), \qquad \omega_n = \beta_n v = \frac{n \pi v}{L}Tn​(t)=Dn​cos(ωn​t)+En​sin(ωn​t),ωn​=βn​v=Lnπv​
(20)

Solution for the spatial part: normal modes¶

  • Because of the boundary conditions X(0)=X(L)=0X(0)=X(L)=0X(0)=X(L)=0 imposed at the ends of the string, we found an infinite number of solutions indexed by an integer nnn. These are the normal modes of the string:

Normal modes of a string fixed at both ends
Xn(x)=Bnsin⁡(nπxL),n=1,2,3,…X_n(x) = B_n \sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{L} \right), \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldotsXn​(x)=Bn​sin(Lnπx​),n=1,2,3,…
(21)

  • The wavelength of the mode follows from kn=βn=nπ/L=2π/λnk_n = \beta_n = n\pi/L = 2\pi/\lambda_nkn​=βn​=nπ/L=2π/λn​, so λn=2L/n\lambda_n = 2L/nλn​=2L/n: a whole number of half-wavelengths must fit between the clamps. This is the “waves have to fit” argument of Chapter 1, now derived rather than postulated.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation

Solution for the temporal part¶

  • For the temporal part there are no boundary conditions: time is free to march on. The solution is a linear combination of sine and cosine with ωn=βnv=nπv/L\omega_n = \beta_n v = n \pi v/Lωn​=βn​v=nπv/L, which a trig identity packages into a single cosine with an amplitude and a phase:

Tn(t)=Dncos⁡(ωnt)+Ensin⁡(ωnt)=Ancos⁡(ωnt+ϕn)T_n(t) = D_n \cos(\omega_n t) + E_n \sin(\omega_n t) = A_n \cos (\omega_n t + \phi_n)Tn​(t)=Dn​cos(ωn​t)+En​sin(ωn​t)=An​cos(ωn​t+ϕn​)
(22)

  • Each mode has its own frequency, and the frequencies are integer multiples of the fundamental ω1=πv/L\omega_1 = \pi v/Lω1​=πv/L. This is special to the string; a drumhead or an atom does not have equally spaced frequencies.

  • The constants AnA_nAn​ and ϕn\phi_nϕn​ are not fixed by the equation or by the boundary conditions. They are determined by the initial conditions: where the string is and how fast it is moving at t=0t=0t=0.

Step 3: Full solution as a sum of normal modes¶

  • Each product Xn(x)Tn(t)X_n(x)T_n(t)Xn​(x)Tn​(t) is a standing wave that solves the wave equation and respects the clamps. By superposition, so does any sum of them, and the sum over all nnn is general enough to describe every possible motion of the string:

General solution for a string fixed at both ends
u(x,t)=∑n=1∞Xn(x)Tn(t)=∑n=1∞Ansin⁡(nπxL)cos⁡(ωnt+ϕn),ωn=nπvLu(x, t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} X_n(x) T_n(t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} A_n \sin \left(\frac{n \pi x}{L} \right) \cos (\omega_n t + \phi_n), \qquad \omega_n = \frac{n\pi v}{L}u(x,t)=n=1∑∞​Xn​(x)Tn​(t)=n=1∑∞​An​sin(Lnπx​)cos(ωn​t+ϕn​),ωn​=Lnπv​
(23)

  • xxx: position along the string, confined to [0,L][0, L][0,L]

  • ttt: time, free on [0,∞)[0, \infty)[0,∞)

  • n=1,2,3,…n = 1, 2, 3, \ldotsn=1,2,3,…: index of the normal mode

  • AnA_nAn​, ϕn\phi_nϕn​: amplitude and phase of each mode, set by the initial conditions

  • The normal modes Xn(x)X_n(x)Xn​(x) are a property of the string alone (its length and its clamps). How much of each mode is present, the AnA_nAn​ and ϕn\phi_nϕn​, depends on how and where the string is plucked.

About nodes¶

Places where the string stays at rest are called nodes. Their number grows with nnn:

  • n=1n = 1n=1: no interior node. This is the fundamental or first harmonic.

  • n=2n = 2n=2: one node at x=L/2x = L/2x=L/2. The first overtone or second harmonic.

  • n=3n = 3n=3: two nodes at L/3L/3L/3 and 2L/32L/32L/3. The second overtone or third harmonic.

A single mode is a standing wave with fixed nodes. A sum of modes is not: because the modes oscillate at different frequencies, the points of zero displacement move around, and the shape changes from instant to instant.

L, v = 1.0, 1.0

ts = np.linspace(0, 2 * L / v, 40, endpoint=False)     # one period of the fundamental

Tt = lambda n, t: np.cos(n * np.pi * v * t / L)
combos = [[1], [3], [1, 2], [1, 2, 3]]

Initial conditions pick the amplitudes: the plucked string¶

  • The normal modes are fixed by the string; the amplitudes AnA_nAn​ and phases ϕn\phi_nϕn​ are fixed by how it is set in motion. Suppose the string is pulled into a shape u(x,0)=f(x)u(x,0)=f(x)u(x,0)=f(x) and released from rest, so that ∂u/∂t=0\partial u/\partial t = 0∂u/∂t=0 at t=0t=0t=0. Zero initial velocity kills every sin⁡(ωnt)\sin(\omega_n t)sin(ωn​t) term, i.e. all ϕn=0\phi_n = 0ϕn​=0, and the shape condition reads

f(x)=∑n=1∞Ansin⁡(nπxL)f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty A_n \sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)f(x)=n=1∑∞​An​sin(Lnπx​)
(24)

  • To extract a single AmA_mAm​, multiply both sides by sin⁡(mπx/L)\sin(m\pi x/L)sin(mπx/L) and integrate over the string. The sine modes are orthogonal:

∫0Lsin⁡(nπxL)sin⁡(mπxL)dx={L/2n=m0n≠m\int_0^L \sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\sin\left(\frac{m\pi x}{L}\right)dx = \begin{cases} L/2 & n = m \\ 0 & n \neq m \end{cases}∫0L​sin(Lnπx​)sin(Lmπx​)dx={L/20​n=mn=m​
(25)

so every term of the sum vanishes except the one with n=mn=mn=m:

Mode amplitudes from the initial shape
An=2L∫0Lf(x) sin⁡(nπxL)dxA_n = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L f(x)\,\sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)dxAn​=L2​∫0L​f(x)sin(Lnπx​)dx
(26)

  • This is a Fourier sine series (Appendix A.6). The move “multiply by a mode and integrate, orthogonality does the rest” is the single most reused calculation in this course: in Chapter 3 it expands a quantum state in eigenfunctions, and the AnA_nAn​ become probability amplitudes.

Example: a string plucked off center

Pull the string at x=ax=ax=a up to height hhh and let go. The initial shape is a triangle, f=hx/af = hx/af=hx/a for x<ax<ax<a and f=h(L−x)/(L−a)f=h(L-x)/(L-a)f=h(L−x)/(L−a) for x>ax>ax>a. Integrating by parts (or with SymPy) gives

An=2hL2π2n2 a(L−a)sin⁡(nπaL)A_n = \frac{2hL^2}{\pi^2 n^2\, a(L-a)}\sin\left(\frac{n\pi a}{L}\right)An​=π2n2a(L−a)2hL2​sin(Lnπa​)
(27)

Two lessons sit in this formula. The amplitudes fall off as 1/n21/n^21/n2, so a handful of modes carries most of the motion. And An=0A_n = 0An​=0 whenever sin⁡(nπa/L)=0\sin(n\pi a/L)=0sin(nπa/L)=0: a mode with a node at the pluck point is not excited. Plucking at a=L/3a = L/3a=L/3 silences n=3,6,9,…n=3,6,9,\ldotsn=3,6,9,…; plucking at the midpoint silences every even harmonic; in the animation below, plucked at a=0.3La = 0.3La=0.3L, the tenth harmonic is missing.

# synced: plucked_string
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
L, v, h, a = 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.3            # length, speed, pluck height, pluck position
N = 40                                      # modes kept
n = np.arange(1, N + 1)
A = 2 * h * L**2 * np.sin(n * np.pi * a / L) / (np.pi**2 * n**2 * a * (L - a))
x = np.linspace(0, L, 600)
modes = np.sin(np.outer(n, np.pi * x / L))
omega = n * np.pi * v / L
ts = np.linspace(0, 2 * L / v, 40, endpoint=False)
f0 = np.where(x < a, h * x / a, h * (L - x) / (L - a))

fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(7.5, 5.8), gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.5, 1]})
ax.plot(x, f0, color=GRAY, lw=1.2, ls=":", label="initial pluck")
(u,) = ax.plot([], [], color=CARDINAL, lw=2.8, label=r"$u(x,t)=\sum_n A_n \sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\cos\omega_n t$")
(m1,) = ax.plot([], [], color=TEAL, lw=1.4, ls="--", label="n = 1 term")
(m2,) = ax.plot([], [], color=ORANGE, lw=1.4, ls="--", label="n = 2 term")
ax.plot([0, L], [0, 0], "o", color=GRAY, ms=7); ax.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.6)
ax.set_xlim(-0.02, L + 0.02); ax.set_ylim(-1.15, 1.45); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.set_xlabel("x")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False, fontsize=9.5, ncol=2)
ax.set_title("a string plucked at x = 0.3 L, rebuilt from its normal modes", loc="left", fontsize=11.5)
bx.bar(n[:12], A[:12], color=[TEAL if c >= 0 else ORANGE for c in A[:12]], width=0.7)
bx.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.6)
bx.set_xticks(n[:12]); bx.set_xlabel("mode n"); bx.set_ylabel(r"$A_n$")
bx.set_title(r"the pluck sets the recipe:  $A_n = \frac{2hL^2}{\pi^2 n^2 a(L-a)}\sin\frac{n\pi a}{L}$",
             loc="left", fontsize=11.5)
fig.tight_layout()

def update(i):
    Tn = np.cos(omega * ts[i])
    u.set_data(x, (A * Tn) @ modes)
    m1.set_data(x, A[0] * Tn[0] * modes[0]); m2.set_data(x, A[1] * Tn[1] * modes[1])

ani = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=len(ts), interval=90, blit=False)
plt.close(fig)

The notes of a string¶

  • Each normal mode oscillates at ωn=nπv/L\omega_n = n\pi v/Lωn​=nπv/L, so the frequencies a string can sound are

Harmonics of a string fixed at both ends
νn=ωn2π=n v2L,n=1,2,3,…\nu_n = \frac{\omega_n}{2\pi} = n\,\frac{v}{2L}, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldotsνn​=2πωn​​=n2Lv​,n=1,2,3,…
(28)

  • The fundamental ν1=v/2L\nu_1 = v/2Lν1​=v/2L sets the pitch. The harmonics (overtones) are its integer multiples, and their mix, the AnA_nAn​ of the previous section, sets the timbre that tells a guitar from a piano playing the same note.

Example: tuning and fretting a guitar

The low E string of a guitar has L=0.65 mL = 0.65\ \text{m}L=0.65 m and sounds at ν1=82.4 Hz\nu_1 = 82.4\ \text{Hz}ν1​=82.4 Hz.

  • A. Wave speed on the string. From ν1=v/2L\nu_1 = v/2Lν1​=v/2L: v=2Lν1=2(0.65 m)(82.4 s−1)=107 m/sv = 2L\nu_1 = 2(0.65\ \text{m})(82.4\ \text{s}^{-1}) = 107\ \text{m/s}v=2Lν1​=2(0.65 m)(82.4 s−1)=107 m/s.

  • B. First two overtones. ν2=2ν1=164.8 Hz\nu_2 = 2\nu_1 = 164.8\ \text{Hz}ν2​=2ν1​=164.8 Hz and ν3=3ν1=247.2 Hz\nu_3 = 3\nu_1 = 247.2\ \text{Hz}ν3​=3ν1​=247.2 Hz.

  • C. Fretting. Pressing the string at the 12th fret halves its length. With L→L/2L \to L/2L→L/2 and vvv unchanged, the fundamental doubles to 164.8 Hz164.8\ \text{Hz}164.8 Hz: one octave up.

  • D. Tuning. Tightening the string raises vvv (for a string v=T/μv = \sqrt{\mathcal{T}/\mu}v=T/μ​, tension over mass per unit length), which raises every νn\nu_nνn​ in proportion.

2D membrane vibrations¶

  • A drumhead is a 2D membrane with fixed edges. Its displacement u(x,y,t)u(x, y, t)u(x,y,t) depends on two spatial variables, and separation of variables now uses a product of three functions:

u(x,y,t)=X(x) Y(y) T(t)u(x, y, t) = X(x)\, Y(y)\, T(t)u(x,y,t)=X(x)Y(y)T(t)
(29)

  • The boundary conditions on a rectangular membrane of sides aaa and bbb pin each spatial factor at its two edges: X(0)=X(a)=0X(0) = X(a) = 0X(0)=X(a)=0 and Y(0)=Y(b)=0Y(0) = Y(b) = 0Y(0)=Y(b)=0. Each factor is therefore a 1D normal mode, and the 2D mode is their product, labeled by two integers nnn and mmm:

u(x,y,t)=∑n∑mAnmcos⁡(ωnmt+ϕnm)sin⁡(nπxa)sin⁡(mπyb)u(x, y, t) = \sum_n \sum_m A_{nm} \cos(\omega_{nm}t + \phi_{nm}) \sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{a}\right) \sin\left(\frac{m\pi y}{b}\right)u(x,y,t)=n∑​m∑​Anm​cos(ωnm​t+ϕnm​)sin(anπx​)sin(bmπy​)
(30)

  • The frequency of a mode depends on both integers and on the geometry:

Frequencies of a rectangular membrane
ωnm=vπ(n2a2+m2b2)1/2\omega_{nm} = v\pi \left(\frac{n^2}{a^2} + \frac{m^2}{b^2}\right)^{1/2}ωnm​=vπ(a2n2​+b2m2​)1/2
(31)

  • Unlike the string, the frequencies are not integer multiples of the lowest one. This is why a drum has no definite pitch while a string does.

Fig. The four lowest normal modes of a square membrane, all shown at a common phase so that the shapes can be compared. Each is a product of a sine in xxx and a sine in yyy; the nodal lines where the membrane stays flat are the 2D counterpart of the nodes on a string.

Degeneracy

For a square membrane (a=ba=ba=b) the modes (2,1)(2,1)(2,1) and (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) have the same frequency although their shapes differ: one has its nodal line along yyy, the other along xxx. Distinct modes that share one frequency are called degenerate. Degeneracy is always a sign of symmetry, here the interchangeability of the xxx and yyy directions; stretch the membrane into a rectangle and the two frequencies split. Degeneracy returns for the particle in a 2D box and, in a more elaborate form, for the orbitals of the hydrogen atom.

Use the sliders to choose the two mode numbers and rotate the surface.

Full derivation of the 2D rectangular membrane problem

Consider a rectangular membrane with dimensions LxL_xLx​ and LyL_yLy​, fixed along its edges. The wave equation for the membrane is

∂2u∂t2=v2(∂2u∂x2+∂2u∂y2)\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = v^2 \left( \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y^2} \right)∂t2∂2u​=v2(∂x2∂2u​+∂y2∂2u​)
(32)

Separation of variables. Assume u(x,y,t)=X(x)Y(y)T(t)u(x, y, t) = X(x) Y(y) T(t)u(x,y,t)=X(x)Y(y)T(t), substitute, and divide through by XYTX Y TXYT:

1v21Td2Tdt2=1Xd2Xdx2+1Yd2Ydy2\frac{1}{v^2} \frac{1}{T} \frac{d^2 T}{dt^2} = \frac{1}{X} \frac{d^2 X}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{Y} \frac{d^2 Y}{dy^2}v21​T1​dt2d2T​=X1​dx2d2X​+Y1​dy2d2Y​
(33)

The left side depends only on ttt, the right side only on xxx and yyy, so both equal a constant, which we call −λ-\lambda−λ. On the right, the xxx term and the yyy term must in turn each be constant, −α2-\alpha^2−α2 and −β2-\beta^2−β2, with α2+β2=λ\alpha^2 + \beta^2 = \lambdaα2+β2=λ. This gives three ODEs:

d2Xdx2+α2X=0,d2Ydy2+β2Y=0,d2Tdt2+λv2T=0\frac{d^2 X}{dx^2} + \alpha^2 X = 0, \qquad \frac{d^2 Y}{dy^2} + \beta^2 Y = 0, \qquad \frac{d^2 T}{dt^2} + \lambda v^2 T = 0dx2d2X​+α2X=0,dy2d2Y​+β2Y=0,dt2d2T​+λv2T=0
(34)

Boundary conditions. X(0)=X(Lx)=0X(0) = X(L_x) = 0X(0)=X(Lx​)=0 and Y(0)=Y(Ly)=0Y(0) = Y(L_y) = 0Y(0)=Y(Ly​)=0 quantize α\alphaα and β\betaβ exactly as for the string:

Xn(x)=sin⁡(nπxLx),αn=nπLx,Ym(y)=sin⁡(mπyLy),βm=mπLyX_n(x) = \sin\left(\frac{n \pi x}{L_x}\right), \quad \alpha_n = \frac{n\pi}{L_x}, \qquad Y_m(y) = \sin\left(\frac{m \pi y}{L_y}\right), \quad \beta_m = \frac{m\pi}{L_y}Xn​(x)=sin(Lx​nπx​),αn​=Lx​nπ​,Ym​(y)=sin(Ly​mπy​),βm​=Ly​mπ​
(35)

Time part. With λnm=αn2+βm2\lambda_{nm} = \alpha_n^2 + \beta_m^2λnm​=αn2​+βm2​, TTT oscillates at ωnm=vλnm\omega_{nm} = v\sqrt{\lambda_{nm}}ωnm​=vλnm​​.

General solution.

u(x,y,t)=∑n=1∞∑m=1∞[Anmcos⁡(ωnmt)+Bnmsin⁡(ωnmt)]sin⁡(nπxLx)sin⁡(mπyLy),ωnm=vπn2Lx2+m2Ly2u(x, y, t) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \sum_{m=1}^\infty \left[ A_{nm} \cos\left(\omega_{nm} t\right) + B_{nm} \sin\left(\omega_{nm} t\right) \right] \sin\left(\frac{n \pi x}{L_x}\right) \sin\left(\frac{m \pi y}{L_y}\right), \qquad \omega_{nm} = v \pi\sqrt{\frac{n^2}{L_x^2} + \frac{m^2}{L_y^2}}u(x,y,t)=n=1∑∞​m=1∑∞​[Anm​cos(ωnm​t)+Bnm​sin(ωnm​t)]sin(Lx​nπx​)sin(Ly​mπy​),ωnm​=vπLx2​n2​+Ly2​m2​​
(36)

The sound of music¶

  • The sound of a musical instrument is a superposition of its normal modes (the harmonics or overtones of music). Which modes are present, and how strongly, depends on how the instrument is excited: where a string is plucked, where a drum is struck.

  • Learn more from this series.

Looking ahead: the same recipe for the Schrödinger equation¶

Everything in this lecture transfers to quantum mechanics with a change of cast. Keep this table in mind when Chapter 3 solves the particle in a box.

classical stringquantum particle in a box
wave equation uxx=utt/v2u_{xx} = u_{tt}/v^2uxx​=utt​/v2Schrödinger equation −ℏ22mΨxx+VΨ=iℏΨt-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\Psi_{xx} + V\Psi = i\hbar\Psi_t−2mℏ2​Ψxx​+VΨ=iℏΨt​
separation u=X(x) T(t)u = X(x)\,T(t)u=X(x)T(t)separation Ψ=ψ(x) e−iEt/ℏ\Psi = \psi(x)\,e^{-iEt/\hbar}Ψ=ψ(x)e−iEt/ℏ
fixed ends X(0)=X(L)=0X(0)=X(L)=0X(0)=X(L)=0impenetrable walls ψ(0)=ψ(L)=0\psi(0)=\psi(L)=0ψ(0)=ψ(L)=0
normal modes sin⁡(nπx/L)\sin(n\pi x/L)sin(nπx/L)stationary states sin⁡(nπx/L)\sin(n\pi x/L)sin(nπx/L)
frequencies ωn∝n\omega_n \propto nωn​∝nenergies En∝n2E_n \propto n^2En​∝n2
pluck sets the amplitudes AnA_nAn​initial state sets the probability amplitudes cnc_ncn​
orthogonality extracts AnA_nAn​orthogonality extracts cnc_ncn​

The only structural difference is the single time derivative and the factor iii in the Schrödinger equation, which is why quantum “oscillation” in time is a rotating complex phase rather than a real cosine.

Problems¶

Problem 1: Simple harmonic oscillator¶

Solve the ODE

d2ydt2+ω2y=0\frac{d^2 y}{dt^2} + \omega^2 y = 0dt2d2y​+ω2y=0
(37)

where ω\omegaω is a constant.

Solution

The characteristic equation is

r2+ω2=0⟹r=±iωr^2 + \omega^2 = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad r = \pm i \omegar2+ω2=0⟹r=±iω
(38)

Thus the general solution is

y(t)=C1cos⁡(ωt)+C2sin⁡(ωt)y(t) = C_1 \cos(\omega t) + C_2 \sin(\omega t)y(t)=C1​cos(ωt)+C2​sin(ωt)
(39)

where C1C_1C1​ and C2C_2C2​ are constants determined by initial conditions.

Problem 2: Damped oscillator¶

Solve the ODE

d2ydt2+2βdydt+ω2y=0\frac{d^2 y}{dt^2} + 2 \beta \frac{dy}{dt} + \omega^2 y = 0dt2d2y​+2βdtdy​+ω2y=0
(40)

where β\betaβ and ω\omegaω are constants. Consider the cases β2<ω2\beta^2 < \omega^2β2<ω2, β2>ω2\beta^2 > \omega^2β2>ω2, and β2=ω2\beta^2 = \omega^2β2=ω2.

Solution

The characteristic equation is

r2+2βr+ω2=0⟹r=−β±β2−ω2r^2 + 2 \beta r + \omega^2 = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad r = -\beta \pm \sqrt{\beta^2 - \omega^2}r2+2βr+ω2=0⟹r=−β±β2−ω2​
(41)

Depending on the sign of the discriminant β2−ω2\beta^2 - \omega^2β2−ω2 there are three cases:

  1. Underdamping (β2<ω2\beta^2 < \omega^2β2<ω2): the roots are complex, r=−β±iωdr = -\beta \pm i\omega_dr=−β±iωd​ with ωd=ω2−β2\omega_d = \sqrt{\omega^2 - \beta^2}ωd​=ω2−β2​, giving a decaying oscillation

    y(t)=e−βt[C1cos⁡(ωdt)+C2sin⁡(ωdt)]y(t) = e^{-\beta t} [C_1 \cos(\omega_d t) + C_2 \sin(\omega_d t)]y(t)=e−βt[C1​cos(ωd​t)+C2​sin(ωd​t)]
    (42)

  2. Critical damping (β2=ω2\beta^2 = \omega^2β2=ω2): a repeated root r=−βr = -\betar=−β,

    y(t)=(C1+C2t)e−βty(t) = (C_1 + C_2 t) e^{-\beta t}y(t)=(C1​+C2​t)e−βt
    (43)

  3. Overdamping (β2>ω2\beta^2 > \omega^2β2>ω2): two distinct real (negative) roots r1,r2r_1, r_2r1​,r2​,

    y(t)=C1er1t+C2er2ty(t) = C_1 e^{r_1 t} + C_2 e^{r_2 t}y(t)=C1​er1​t+C2​er2​t
    (44)

Problem 3: Real roots¶

Solve the ODE

d2ydt2−4y=0\frac{d^2 y}{dt^2} - 4 y = 0dt2d2y​−4y=0
(45)
Solution

The characteristic equation is r2−4=0r^2 - 4 = 0r2−4=0, so r=±2r = \pm 2r=±2 and

y(t)=C1e2t+C2e−2ty(t) = C_1 e^{2t} + C_2 e^{-2t}y(t)=C1​e2t+C2​e−2t
(46)

Real roots give exponentials, not oscillations. Compare with Problem 4, where the sign of the constant term is flipped.

Problem 4: Imaginary roots¶

Solve the ODE

d2ydt2+9y=0\frac{d^2 y}{dt^2} + 9 y = 0dt2d2y​+9y=0
(47)
Solution

The characteristic equation is r2+9=0r^2 + 9 = 0r2+9=0, so r=±3ir = \pm 3ir=±3i and

y(t)=C1cos⁡(3t)+C2sin⁡(3t)y(t) = C_1 \cos(3t) + C_2 \sin(3t)y(t)=C1​cos(3t)+C2​sin(3t)
(48)

Problem 5: Repeated roots¶

Solve the ODE

d2ydt2−6dydt+9y=0\frac{d^2 y}{dt^2} - 6 \frac{dy}{dt} + 9 y = 0dt2d2y​−6dtdy​+9y=0
(49)
Solution

The characteristic equation factors as (r−3)2=0(r - 3)^2 = 0(r−3)2=0, a repeated root r=3r = 3r=3. The general solution for repeated roots is

y(t)=(C1+C2t)e3ty(t) = (C_1 + C_2 t) e^{3t}y(t)=(C1​+C2​t)e3t
(50)

Problem 6: A string with one free end¶

A string of length LLL is clamped at x=0x=0x=0 but its other end slides freely on a frictionless rod, so that the slope vanishes there: X(0)=0X(0) = 0X(0)=0 and X′(L)=0X'(L) = 0X′(L)=0. Find the allowed normal modes and their frequencies. Which harmonics of the fixed-fixed string are missing? (A clarinet, closed at one end and open at the other, has the same pattern.)

Problem 7: Plucking at the midpoint¶

A string is pulled to height hhh at its midpoint and released from rest. Using the formula for AnA_nAn​ in the plucked-string example, compute A1A_1A1​ through A5A_5A5​ in units of hhh. Which modes are absent, and why can you predict that from the symmetry of the initial shape without any integration?

Problem 8: Frequencies of a square drum¶

For a square membrane of side aaa, list ωnm/ω11\omega_{nm}/\omega_{11}ωnm​/ω11​ for all n,m≤3n, m \leq 3n,m≤3 in increasing order. Which frequencies are degenerate? Now make the membrane rectangular with b=1.2ab = 1.2ab=1.2a: which degeneracies survive?

Problem 9: Waves on a ring¶

A wave travels on a closed loop of circumference LLL, so instead of fixed ends the solution must satisfy periodic boundary conditions, X(0)=X(L)X(0) = X(L)X(0)=X(L) and X′(0)=X′(L)X'(0) = X'(L)X′(0)=X′(L). Show that X(x)=eikxX(x) = e^{ikx}X(x)=eikx works when k=2πn/Lk = 2\pi n/Lk=2πn/L with n=0,±1,±2,…n = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldotsn=0,±1,±2,…, find the wavelengths, and compare with the standing-wave condition on a Bohr orbit in Chapter 1.

Problem 10: Orthogonality of the modes¶

Show by direct integration that

∫0Lsin⁡(nπxL)sin⁡(mπxL)dx=L2 δnm\int_0^L \sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\sin\left(\frac{m\pi x}{L}\right)dx = \frac{L}{2}\,\delta_{nm}∫0L​sin(Lnπx​)sin(Lmπx​)dx=2L​δnm​
(51)

for positive integers n,mn, mn,m. (Use sin⁡αsin⁡β=12[cos⁡(α−β)−cos⁡(α+β)]\sin\alpha\sin\beta = \tfrac{1}{2}[\cos(\alpha-\beta)-\cos(\alpha+\beta)]sinαsinβ=21​[cos(α−β)−cos(α+β)].) Then use the result to verify the formula An=2L∫0Lf(x)sin⁡(nπx/L) dxA_n = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L f(x)\sin(n\pi x/L)\,dxAn​=L2​∫0L​f(x)sin(nπx/L)dx.
